standard.title: Sequence making steps cooperatively
standard.description: sequence steps for making designed solutions cooperatively
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use materials and equipment to make solutions (AC9TDEFP01, AC9TDE2P02). They have followed steps to make things. They have not yet formally sequenced steps for making as a planning activity, recorded procedures, or identified roles for cooperative group making.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students sequence the steps for making a designed solution and work cooperatively with others, identifying roles within a group.

nodes.label: Sequencing making steps
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can sequence the steps needed to make a designed solution in a logical order
nodes.minimum_width: Sequence at least four steps for making a simple product in the correct order; explain why the order matters
nodes.typical_width: Use lists or storyboarding to plan and sequence steps for making across different production contexts; record the procedure; explain why steps must be in a particular order and what happens if they are not
wider: Record the ordered steps for making a salad or other food preparation task — describe each step and explain what would happen if the order changed
Create a planning list or storyboard for an electronic planting calendar — sequence the steps and explain the order decisions

response_modes.reason: Step sequencing in design feels obvious for simple tasks but students often conflate steps with materials or confuse what to do with when to do it. Multiple production contexts — food preparation (where order is safety-critical), construction (where joins must be made before assembly), garden tasks — each expose different dimensions of why sequence matters.

success_criteria: Sequences at least four steps in a logical order
Can explain why at least one step must come before another
nodes.hinge_reason: Step sequencing is the planning input for Node 2's cooperative role assignment — without a sequence to distribute across group members, roles cannot be meaningfully identified and the cooperative making has no structure.

nodes.label: Working cooperatively with identified roles
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify roles for group members and work cooperatively toward a shared making outcome
nodes.minimum_width: Participate in a cooperative making task where roles are identified; carry out at least one assigned role
nodes.typical_width: Identify roles for each group member appropriate to the task; work cooperatively toward a shared goal; adjust roles or steps as needed when problems arise
wider: Make a number of items for a school event with a group — assign roles (cutting, joining, decorating, checking), carry out the assigned role and explain how each role contributes to the shared outcome
Write instructions for making a container or bag — include who does each step (role) and in what order; test whether another group can follow the instructions

response_modes.reason: Cooperative making requires students to coordinate sequenced steps (node 1) with distributed roles — two understandings that must work together. Integration failure looks like: students who can sequence steps individually but cannot coordinate with others (duplicating work, waiting, doing steps in the wrong order because communication broke down).

success_criteria: Carries out an identified role in a cooperative making task
The group's shared output is produced — the cooperative process functioned
